newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope says peace possible only with forgiveness.
newsitem.headline: Pope says peace possible only with forgiveness.

text.p: Pope John Paul has called for the granting of amnesties after armed conflict as a way to consolidate peace.

In a message released on Tuesday to mark the Roman Catholic Church's World Peace Day the 76-year-old Pontiff urged a spirit of forgiveness to heal the wounds of ethnic, religious, cultural and spiritual conflict and end what he called "the deadly cycle of revenge".
"Offering and accepting forgiveness is the essential condition for making the journey towards authentic and lasting peace," the Pope said in his 18-page message.
World Peace Day falls on January 1 but the Vatican each year releases the Pope's message in advance.
His remarks about amnesty were contained in a section of the message about the need to establish the truth about what happened in a conflict as a basis for restoring peace.
"The evil which has been done must be acknowledged and as far as possible corrected," the Pope wrote, saying this principle had led to the establishment of various truth commissions around the world.

"Not uncommon are cases of countries whose leaders, looking to the fundamental good of consolidating peace, have agreed to grant an amnesty to those who have publicly admitted crimes committed during a period of turmoil," he said.
"Such an initiative can be regarded favourably as an effort to promote good relations between groups previously opposed to one another," he wrote.

The Pope urged people to make a big push for peace as the new millennium approached while acknowledging that history, which carries "a heavy burden of violence and conflict," could not be easily shed.
The Pope, spiritual leader of nearly one billion Roman Catholics, said the teaching of forgiveness to young people was essential if "a culture of war" was to be replaced with "a culture of peace".
"When such forgiveness is lacking, wounds continue to fester, fuelling in the younger generation endless resentment, producing a desire for revenge and causing fresh destruction," the Pope said.
He said steps should be taken to stop the growth of the arms industry and arms trafficking and called on all churches and governments to do more to promote peace.
The Pope singled out the United Nations, saying it had taken on a wider role of international peacekeeping.

"In this regard, 50 years after its establishment, it seems fitting to hope that the means at its disposal will be appropriately reviewed in order to enable that organisation to face effectively the new challenges of our time," he said.
He also said his efforts to secure Christian unity in the run-up to the Roman Catholic Jubilee Year of 2000 could help bring about peace.
"This cannot fail to exercise a positive influence on the peacemaking processes going on in different parts of the world," he said.
